
:::{#def-predicted-value}
#### Predicted value

In a regression model $\p(y|\vx)$, 
the **predicted value** of $y$ given $\vx$ is the estimated mean of $Y$ given $\vX=\vx$:

$$\hat y \eqdef \eExpf{Y|\vX=\vx}$$
:::

---

For linear models, 
the predicted value can be straightforwardly calculated 
by multiplying each predictor value $x_j$ by its corresponding coefficient $\beta_j$ 
and adding up the results:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat y &= \eExpf{Y|\vX=\vx} \\
&= \tp{\vx}\hat\beta \\
&= \hat\beta_0\cdot 1 + \hat\beta_1 x_1 + ... + \hat\beta_p x_p
\end{aligned}
$$

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-fitted-value}
#### Fitted value

For a given dataset $(\vY, \mX)$ and corresponding fitted model $\p_{\eb}(\vy|\mx)$, 
the **fitted value** of $y_i$ is 
the predicted value (see @def-predicted-value) of $y$ when $\vX=\vx_i$ using the estimated parameters $\eb$:

$$\hat y_i \eqdef \eExpf{Y_i|\vX=\vx_i} = \tp{\vxi}\eb$$
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-fitted-vs-predicted}
#### Fitted values versus predicted values

Fitted values and predicted values use the same formula,
but they answer different questions:

- A **fitted value** $\hat y_i$ describes an observation that is already in the dataset.
  Its outcome $y_i$ helped determine $\eb$,
  so the model has already "seen" $y_i$.
- A **predicted value** $\hat y$ describes a new or hypothetical observation
  with covariate vector $\vx$,
  whose outcome was not used to estimate $\eb$
  (and $\vx$ need not match any $\vx_i$ in the data).

Because each observation pulls the fitted line toward itself,
fitted values tend to be closer to their observed outcomes
than predicted values are to the outcomes of new observations.
So the residuals $y_i - \hat y_i$
tend to understate how far off the model's predictions will be for new data.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-fitted-vs-predicted-bw}
#### Fitted versus predicted value for one `birthweight` observation

Take the first observation in the `birthweight` data.
Its fitted value comes from `bw_lm1`, which was estimated using that observation.
To predict the same observation as if it were new,
refit the model without it and predict at its covariate values:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
bw_lm1_data <- model.frame(bw_lm1)
bw_lm1_drop1 <- update(bw_lm1, data = bw_lm1_data[-1, ])
tibble(
  observed = bw_lm1_data$weight[1],
  fitted = fitted(bw_lm1)[[1]],
  predicted_without_obs = predict(bw_lm1_drop1, newdata = bw_lm1_data[1, ])
)
```

The fitted value is closer to the observed weight
than the prediction from the model that never saw this observation.
:::

---

#### Example: prediction for the `birthweight` data

```{r}
x <- c(1, 1, 40)
sum(x * coef(bw_lm1))
```

R has built-in functions for prediction:

```{r}
x <- tibble(age = 40, sex = "male")
bw_lm1 |> predict(newdata = x)
```

If you don't provide `newdata`, 
R will use the covariate values from the original dataset:

```{r}
predict(bw_lm1)
```

These special predictions are called the **fitted values** of the dataset
(see @def-fitted-value).

R has an extra function to get these values:

```{r}
fitted(bw_lm1)
```
